MinneMUDAC 2026 · The Food Group Challenge

Undergraduate division · final team summary of Questions 1, 4, 5, 6 and 7 · built from the main branch on 13 Oct 2026. Every number here matches the executed notebooks and is listed in docs/00_findings_for_slides.md.

The one story

Need is driven by hardship, prices and SNAP. Recorded food shelf demand is driven by access and the food shelf network. Where the two diverge, the cause is mostly access.

  1. Need follows hardship. When prices rise (Q4) or SNAP benefits fall (Q5), more people need help, statewide and about equally everywhere.
  2. Demand follows that pressure over time with a delay (≈15 months after a price surge; 6–10 months after the April 2023 SNAP cut), but across counties it barely follows need per resident (Q1 ρ ≈ 0; Q6 ρ = 0.11).
  3. Where demand is recorded depends on access: distance to a food shelf, whether the nearest one is across the county line, and where the big regional sites are (Q1, Q6). 44 more public factors don't beat this.
  4. So the divergence (Q6) is an access gap: remote rural counties with high need record little; regional hubs record more than their own need.
  5. The forecast (Q7) works because statewide demand is stable; county errors come from local changes such as sites opening or closing.
Q1

Need estimates vs. food shelf activity

Need and food shelf activity agree on county size but not on intensity; where they disagree, distance and cross-county access explain it, not hardship.

Purpose of the question

Do Feeding America's Map the Meal Gap (MMG) county food-insecurity estimates and The Food Group's three food shelf metrics (visits, pounds, individuals) tell the same story for 2022–2024? Which metric tracks need best, which counties break the pattern, and which county characteristics explain the mismatch?

Code & documents

  • notebooks/q1_need_vs_foodshelf_activity.ipynb (main analysis)
  • notebooks/01b_q1_factor_extension.ipynb + docs/01b_q1_factor_extension.md
  • docs/Q1_study_guide.pdf
  • outputs/q1/q1_interactive_maps.html (download and open in a browser)
  • outputs/q1/Q1_slides.pptx, outputs/q1/Q1_presentation_script.pdf
  • Factor tables: notebooks/06a_build_county_factors.ipynb, notebooks/06b_acs_factors.ipynb, notebooks/06c_extra_factors.ipynb

Workflow

  1. Add up food shelf activity per county and year (2022–2024) and join MMG food-insecure people and rates by county FIPS.
  2. Correlate need with each metric, as totals and per resident, every year (Pearson and Spearman).
  3. Estimate each county's expected activity from counties with a similar number of food-insecure people (Method A, confirmed with Methods B and C). Gap = actual ÷ expected.
  4. Shortlist counties that are ≥ 2× or ≤ ½ of expected on 2+ metrics in 2+ of 3 years, and separate data-quality cases (Douglas, Grant, Stevens).
  5. Test county characteristics: poverty, vehicle access, rural share, SNAP, distance from every neighbourhood to the nearest food shelf, nearest food shelf across the county line, sites per resident, food bank network, commuting, mobile pantries.
  6. Extension (Q1b): test 44 more public factors (SAIPE, BLS, SVI, County Health Rankings, ACS, USDA, DEED, WIC), 224 tests with a multiple-testing (FDR) correction and leave-one-out checks.

Key findings

  • Totals agree, mostly because of county size: Spearman ρ = 0.89–0.92 between food-insecure people and each metric, every year (population alone gives 0.88–0.92).
  • Intensity doesn't: food-insecurity rate vs activity per resident in 2024: ρ = −0.01 (visits), 0.02 (pounds), 0.00 (individuals).
  • Over time both rose: 2022 → 2024, need +25%, visits +46%, pounds +31%, individuals +60%.
  • Pounds tracks need slightly best and individuals least, but the differences are small.
  • 12 counties break the pattern: lower = Nicollet, Pope, Lac qui Parle, Norman, Roseau; higher = Steele, Washington, Rice, Renville, Mahnomen, Pipestone, Olmsted.
  • Strongest explanation: share of residents whose nearest food shelf is in another county (ρ = −0.33). Characteristics explain 22% of the mismatch, 34% with the food bank network.
  • Mobile pantries (suggestive): none of the 10 lower-than-expected counties has one; Cook (48% of residents > 10 miles away, 64% of visits from mobile pantries) records 2.4× expected.
  • 44 more public factors add nothing that survives correction (224 tests, best q = 0.12).

Interpretation

  • County need estimates are a weak guide to where food shelf activity happens; county size and where sites are matter more.
  • Activity is counted where the food shelf is, not where people live: Nicollet looks under-served because its residents use Blue Earth's food shelves.
  • Hardship can't explain the gap because MMG is itself built from hardship. The gap is about how need turns into recorded visits: access.

Recommended action

Plan with per-resident, travel-distance and site-level views, not county totals. Investigate the five persistently low counties with their food banks, and pilot mobile pantry stops in Lac qui Parle, Norman and Roseau, which have none in the data.

Charts

Limitations

  • Associations across 86 counties (Wilkin has no food shelf), not causes.
  • Straight-line distance, not driving distance.
  • Cross-county use is inferred, not observed.
  • MMG is a model estimate; the strongest factor is borderline after correction (q = 0.10–0.12).

Further data needed

  • Client ZIP codes (the single most valuable addition).
  • Driving distance and mobile pantry routes.
  • Food shelf hours and capacity.
Q4

Grocery prices and food shelf activity

Food shelves feel a grocery-price surge about 15 months later, not right away, in all three metrics.

Purpose of the question

Do more people come to food shelves when grocery prices rise? Does the response happen at once or with a delay? Does it appear in all three metrics? Are there other cycles that prices don't explain? The timing lets The Food Group warn food shelves and donors ahead of time.

Code & documents

  • notebooks/04_q4_prices_foodshelf.ipynb
  • docs/04_q4_prices_foodshelf.md (includes the answer on how to choose the delay)
  • Data/processed/cpi_monthly_2019_2026.csv
  • Data/external/bls_cpi/README.md

Workflow

  1. Download BLS CPI-U price series (main: Midwest food at home, CUUR0200SAF11) through July 2026; August 2026 values were dropped before saving.
  2. Build a statewide monthly table of the three metrics using same food shelves only (removes growth from new sites) and compare year-over-year growth with year-over-year inflation.
  3. Lag profile: correlate food shelf growth with inflation 0–24 months earlier, and test against 2,000 fake inflation series that are allowed to pick their own best lag.
  4. Regression with the delay chosen by a fixed rule (AIC, BIC, cross-validation) and the SNAP benefit cut as a control (separates prices from SNAP).
  5. Seasonal profile per reporting food shelf, plus a calendar effect (number of weekdays per month).
  6. Robustness: U.S. and Minneapolis prices, all sites vs same sites, dropping flagged rows, 2024+ only.

Key findings

  • Midwest grocery inflation peaked at 15.2% in Aug 2022; same-food-shelf visit growth peaked at +49% in Feb 2024. Grocery prices are 28.5% higher than in Jan 2021 and never fell.
  • No same-month link (visits −0.06, individuals +0.19, pounds +0.10). Best delay 15 months for all three (0.78 / 0.89 / 0.83); likely range 12–17 months.
  • Beats chance for individuals (p = 0.008) and pounds (p = 0.016); borderline for visits (p = 0.064).
  • With the SNAP cut in the model, individuals and pounds keep their full price effect; visits keep about half, so SNAP and prices share the visit spike.
  • Pounds per visit fell from 61 lb (2022) to 50 lb (2025): more visits, less food each.
  • Other cycles: August busiest (+5%), Oct–Nov high, December lowest for visits (−8%); each extra weekday adds ≈3%.

Interpretation

  • A price surge is an early warning with about a year's lead: demand starts rising ~6 months later and peaks 12–17 months later.
  • Pounds reflect supply as well as demand.
  • Overall inflation lines up about as well as grocery inflation, so say "rising prices, led by groceries".

Recommended action

Track Midwest food-at-home and all-items CPI monthly (free, released mid-month). Raise food and funds in the year after a surge and watch pounds per visit as a rationing signal. All-items inflation reached 5.0% in May 2026 (gasoline), so prepare for above-normal growth from about mid-2027 if it persists.

Charts

Limitations

  • Essentially one inflation episode (2021–23); a strong pattern, not proof of cause.
  • Only 43 months of overlapping year-over-year data.
  • Overlaps with the SNAP cut and the end of other pandemic-era help, so effect sizes are upper bounds.
  • Prices are regional (Midwest), not Minnesota-only.

Further data needed

  • A second price episode (more time).
  • Food bank inventory / TEFAP supply data to separate supply from demand in pounds.
Q5

SNAP enrollment and food shelf use

When SNAP benefits per person fell almost 40% in April 2023, food shelf visits grew much faster for a year, everywhere, while SNAP enrollment barely moved.

Purpose of the question

Do SNAP and food shelves move together, or does one replace the other? What happens to food shelf activity when SNAP benefits change? Does the relationship differ across locations? The answer helps The Food Group explain the importance of SNAP to lawmakers.

Code & documents

  • notebooks/05_q5_snap_foodshelf.ipynb
  • docs/05_q5_snap_foodshelf.md
  • docs/q5_plan.md
  • Data/processed/snap_2022_2026_clean.csv

Workflow

  1. Clean MN DHS monthly SNAP reports (cases, people, dollars by county agency, Jan 2022 – Mar 2026) and match agencies to counties (12 shared or tribal-agency counties handled separately).
  2. Together or replace: compare year-over-year changes in SNAP and food shelf use statewide, and SNAP vs visits per resident across counties.
  3. Benefit change: the April 2023 end of the SNAP emergency boost. Compare year-over-year visit growth before, in the year after, and two years after; repeat with same food shelves only.
  4. Location: does visit growth rise with SNAP dollars lost per resident (66 counties)? Also rural vs urban.
  5. Check the 2025–26 enrollment drop (−4%).

Key findings

  • Benefit per person fell from $260 to $160 a month (Mar → Apr 2023).
  • Mar 2022 → Mar 2026: SNAP enrollment −3%, food shelf visits +92%, individuals +99%; month-to-month link ≈ 0.
  • Visit growth before / year after / two years after the cut: +21% / +31% / +8%; same food shelves only: +11% / +31% / +10%. Peak 6–10 months after the cut.
  • Counties that lost more SNAP per resident did not grow faster (ρ = +0.01, p = 0.97).
  • Combined with Q4: the SNAP cut and high inflation overlap; the cut accounts for about half of the visit spike.

Interpretation

  • SNAP and food shelves are neither substitutes nor simple partners at county level: food shelf growth came from beyond SNAP enrollment.
  • Benefit levels matter, not only who is enrolled.
  • The jump was statewide and similar everywhere, so the cut is one important contributor alongside prices, not the only cause.

Recommended action

Treat any SNAP benefit cut as an early warning (more visitors over the next 6–12 months), prepare everywhere rather than only high-SNAP counties, and tell lawmakers that benefit levels drive food shelf demand.

Charts

Limitations

  • No untouched comparison group (the cut hit all of Minnesota at once).
  • The 'before' period is only 3 months.
  • SNAP is reported by county office (12 counties handled specially).
  • SNAP data ends March 2026.

Further data needed

  • SNAP by county of residence, plus applications and closures.
  • Household-level SNAP status of food shelf visitors.
Q6

A divergence measure for need and demand

Fourteen mostly rural counties, led by Swift, Nobles, Wadena, Chippewa and Norman, have need far above their food shelf activity, and distance explains much of it.

Purpose of the question

Create a measure that highlights where need is likely larger than food shelf activity shows. Compare it with the three metrics, find where they diverge, and investigate which county characteristics explain the disagreement. The measure must use more than demand data.

Code & documents

  • notebooks/06_q6_divergence.ipynb
  • docs/06_q6_divergence.md
  • Data/processed/q6_county_need_divergence.csv (one row per county, all scores)
  • outputs/q6/q6_top10_potentially_underserved.csv

Workflow

  1. Need index: equal-weight average of 8 public hardship indicators: MMG food insecurity, deep poverty, median income (reversed), unemployment, low-income housing cost burden, disability, children in single-parent homes, uninsured under 65. No food shelf data and no access measures are in it. PCA gives the same ranking (ρ = 0.99), so the simpler version is the headline.
  2. Demand: visits, pounds and individuals per resident (2022–2024), each separately and combined.
  3. Divergence = need percentile − activity percentile. Positive = potentially underserved.
  4. Stability: 16–18 versions (each year, PCA, MMG only, leave one indicator out, drop data-quality counties, reallocate activity to residents' counties, cost-of-living variants).
  5. Meal-gap coverage: food shelf meals (pounds ÷ 1.2) ÷ MMG meal gap (dollar shortfall ÷ cost per meal), 2024.
  6. Explain divergence with access characteristics (distance, cross-county, food bank, grocery access, rurality...) using correlations and a robust regression; validate need with WIC uptake.

Key findings

  • Need and activity per resident barely relate: ρ = 0.11.
  • Potentially underserved (top 5): Swift +83, Nobles +76, Wadena +63, Chippewa +63, Norman +62; then Todd, Aitkin, Clearwater, Grant, Carlton, Benton, Becker, Pine, Morrison. 14 of the top 15 stay in the top 15 in ≥ 75% of method versions.
  • Activity above need: Washington −94, Olmsted −81, Anoka −78, Rice, Steele, Dodge (regional hubs).
  • Meal-gap coverage 2024: statewide 107%, but the median county covers 63% and 24 counties cover less than half (Norman 19%; Steele 266%). Agrees with divergence (ρ = −0.80).
  • What explains it: residents > 10 miles from a food shelf (ρ = +0.52), plus distance to a full-service grocery store (remoteness); model explains 45%. Store counts, closures and cost of living add nothing.
  • Validation: WIC uptake follows need (0.72), not food shelf activity (0.03), so the need is real where activity is low.

Interpretation

  • The gap between need and activity is mainly an access gap: remote rural counties with high need record little; regional hubs record more than their own need.
  • Part of the gap is cross-county use (Nicollet drops out when activity is reassigned to residents' counties); 13 of 15 counties stay.

Recommended action

Prioritise outreach, mobile pantries and capacity checks in the robust underserved counties, starting where residents are far from both food shelves and full-service grocery stores (Swift, Chippewa, Norman, Clearwater, Becker, Marshall; Red Lake has no full-service SNAP store). Partner with WIC clinics as referral points.

Charts

Limitations

  • County averages hide local pockets of need.
  • Small counties (< 10k people) have wide margins; 4 of the top 10 are small.
  • Divergence is relative (ranks), not an absolute shortfall.
  • Tribal food programs not in our data may meet part of the need in Aitkin, Clearwater, Becker, Carlton, Pine.
  • Grant has a data-quality flag; Scott and Stevens coverage is affected by missing reports.

Further data needed

  • Client ZIP codes.
  • Tribal program (FDPIR) participation.
  • WIC 2023–2024.
  • 211 food-help requests by county.
Q7

Forecast August 2026 activity

We forecast about 238,000 visits, 13.0 million pounds and 739,000 individuals for August 2026, with county errors about 40% below last-year's-August.

Purpose of the question

Predict August 2026 visits, pounds and individuals for each Minnesota county using only information available through July 31, 2026. Using any August data from any source disqualifies the team.

Code & documents

  • forecast_august_2026/README.md
  • forecast_august_2026/submission/make_submission.py (final model)
  • forecast_august_2026/submission/Undergraduate_Predictions_Submit.csv (submission file)
  • forecast_august_2026/submission/cutoff_check.txt
  • forecast_august_2026/report/forecasting_report.pdf, forecast_august_2026/report/pipeline_flow.pdf

Workflow

  1. Use only the cleaned food shelf site-month file (no outside predictors); every input is checked to end at July 2026.
  2. Five robust candidate forecasts per county: seasonal naive (last August), damped 3-month year-over-year growth, local-model selection, their blend, and the recent 3-month mean.
  3. County-by-county selection: each county uses whichever candidate had the lowest error on that county over its previous 12 one-month-ahead forecasts.
  4. Backtest over 31 monthly forecast origins (Jan 2024 – Jul 2026), each built only from earlier months.
  5. 101 other models (statistical, panel ML, deep learning, structural) were tested in the same leakage-safe harness; none beat the simple methods out of sample.

Key findings

  • Statewide totals: 237,861 visits (80% range 221,209–258,297), 12,994,439 lb (12.19M–13.62M), 738,532 individuals (697k–802k).
  • County error (WAPE): 9.5% / 8.9% / 9.1% (visits / pounds / individuals) vs 15.3% / 14.5% / 15.4% for last-year's-August; statewide error 4.8% / 3.7% / 4.7%; bias ≈ 0.
  • Visits used the recent mean in 33 counties, damped growth in 21, the blend in 14, seasonal naive in 10, local selection in 8.
  • Cutoff check: every source ends July 2026 and every forecast uses only earlier months (all PASS). Wilkin predicted 0 (no food shelf).

Interpretation

  • Statewide demand is stable month to month; the forecast's main job is to catch local changes such as a site opening or closing (e.g. Mille Lacs gained a site in April 2026).
  • Simple, county-tailored methods beat complex models, which over-fit one period.

Recommended action

Use the county forecasts for August allocation and staffing, re-run monthly with the same script, and treat a county switching to the 'recent mean' method as a sign that something changed locally.

Charts

Limitations

  • One-month-ahead accuracy only.
  • The final method was picked among four county-tailoring variants after seeing results.
  • External predictors (SNAP, hotline calls) were tested and rejected.

Further data needed

  • Site openings, closures and hours known in advance.
  • Planned mobile pantry schedules.
→

Recommendations for The Food Group

  1. Allocation. Allocate on need per resident and distance, not county totals or past visits alone. Use the Q7 county forecasts month to month, and add a buffer about 15 months after a price surge (Q4) and 6–12 months after a SNAP cut (Q5).
  2. Where to add food shelves or mobile pantries. The robust Q6 counties, starting where residents are far from both food shelves and full-service groceries: Swift, Chippewa, Norman, Clearwater, Becker, Marshall, and Red Lake (no full-service SNAP store). Pilot mobile pantries in Lac qui Parle, Norman and Roseau (Q1).
  3. Policy argument. SNAP benefit levels matter: after the April 2023 cut (≈ −40% per person), visits grew 31% in a year at the same food shelves while enrollment barely moved. Price surges hit a year later. Protect benefit levels and fund food shelves ahead of the delay.
  4. Measuring results. Track per county each year: activity per resident, meal-gap coverage, pounds per visit and the Q6 divergence score. Start collecting client ZIP codes so cross-county use can be measured.

✓

August-data compliance

  • No data dated August 2026 or later is used anywhere. Food shelf data ends July 2026; BLS returned August 2026 prices, which were dropped before saving (the Q4 notebook asserts the cutoff); SNAP ends March 2026; SNAP retailer records end December 2025.
  • The Q7 pipeline checks every source and every forecast against the cutoff (forecast_august_2026/submission/cutoff_check.txt: all PASS).
  • A SNAP dashboard file downloaded after the cutoff (with Aug–Sep 2026 months) was removed from the repository; it is not used by any notebook or by the submitted model.
